claims.text: Conventional solid-solution processing of high-entropy alloys produces coarse-grained, homogeneous microstructures with limited phase control.
Deformation at approximately 0.5–0.8 Tm under a controlled strain rate will induce a hierarchical microstructure containing local chemical order and refined subgrains.
Rapid cooling will quench and retain the deformation-induced hierarchical microstructure.
A short-duration anneal will stabilize local chemical order and refined subgrains.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can induce twinning in high-entropy alloys.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can induce dynamic local chemical ordering.
Local chemical order acts as a barrier to dislocation motion and thereby contributes to strengthening.
Refined subgrain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Local chemical order and refined subgrains enable distributed plastic deformation.
The hierarchical microstructure promotes crack deflection.
The proposed treatment will improve yield strength relative to conventional processing.
The proposed treatment will preserve or improve tensile ductility relative to conventional processing.
The proposed treatment will improve Young's modulus relative to conventional processing.
The proposed treatment will improve fracture toughness or fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Yield strength will increase by approximately 10–20% relative to the conventionally processed control.
Young's modulus will increase by approximately 10–20% relative to the conventionally processed control.
The benefits will occur only when deformation is performed within the designated intermediate homologous-temperature range and at controlled strain rates.
Room-temperature deformation or excessively high strain rates may fail to produce the desired hierarchical features.
Prolonged annealing can cause grain growth and eliminate the anticipated performance improvements.
The exact improvements in all four target properties and the robustness of the hierarchy across service conditions remain experimentally unvalidated.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome assigns the approximately 10–20% increase specifically to yield strength and modulus, while requiring only comparable or improved ductility and an unquantified increase in fracture toughness. The falsification rule instead requires yield strength, ductility, modulus, and fracture toughness all to improve by approximately 10–20% across all test conditions.
